terms.definition: A conceptual sequence of stages data passes through—from planning and creation to use, sharing, archiving, and destruction—often with loops and parallel paths.
The system of decision rights, policies, roles, and oversight that directs how an organization manages and uses data as an asset.
The set of practices that develop, protect, deliver, and improve data so it supports organizational goals.
DAMA International’s Data Management Body of Knowledge—a vendor-neutral framework organizing data management into knowledge areas with governance at the center.
In DAMA-DMBOK, one of the major disciplines (such as metadata or data quality) that together describe enterprise data management.
A visual model placing data governance at the hub with other knowledge areas arranged around it to show interdependence.
NIST’s Research Data Framework—a community-informed map of research data management organized around six lifecycle stages and supporting topics.
A USGS model with stages Plan, Acquire, Process, Analyze, Preserve, and Publish/Share, plus cross-cutting describe, quality, and security activities.
Work such as metadata, quality, or security that must continue across multiple lifecycle stages rather than occurring only once.
A role with accountability for decisions about a data domain, including access principles, quality expectations, and policy alignment.
A role that operationalizes governance day to day—maintaining definitions, monitoring quality, and bridging business and technical teams.
A typically technical role that implements storage, security, backups, and access controls according to owner and steward requirements.
A cross-functional body that approves enterprise data standards and resolves conflicts spanning multiple domains.
An executive or senior leader responsible for enterprise data strategy, often including governance coordination and value from data assets.
A responsibility matrix labeling roles as Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, or Informed for each activity.
Explicit authority describing who may approve which kinds of data-related decisions.
A high-level rule set stating required and prohibited behaviors for creating, accessing, sharing, retaining, or disposing of data.
A measurable convention (naming, formats, codes, required metadata) that makes policy enforceable in practice.
Labeling data by sensitivity or criticality so proportionate security and handling rules can apply.
Collecting and keeping only the data that is adequate and necessary for a stated purpose.
Using personal data for specified, legitimate purposes and not for incompatible secondary uses without a proper basis.
Rules stating how long categories of records or data must be kept and when they should be archived or destroyed.
Guiding principles that data and metadata should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable for humans and machines.
A long-lasting unique ID (such as a DOI) used to locate and cite a dataset or digital object reliably over time.
Descriptive information about data—meaning, structure, ownership, lineage, sensitivity, and operational status—that enables discovery and governance.
A curated list of business terms and definitions agreed across teams to reduce ambiguity in metrics and entities.
A searchable inventory of data assets enriched with metadata, ownership, and often usage or quality signals.
Traceability of data from sources through transformations to downstream products, used for impact analysis and trust.
Documented history of how a dataset was created, processed, and by whom—supporting reuse and audit.
The degree to which data is fit for its intended uses, often assessed across multiple dimensions.
A quality dimension measuring how correctly data represents real-world facts or trusted sources.
A quality dimension measuring whether required values and records are present.
A quality dimension measuring whether the same information agrees across systems or records.
A quality dimension measuring whether data is available and sufficiently current when needed.
A quality dimension measuring conformance to formats, ranges, and defined business rules.
A quality dimension measuring the absence of unintended duplicate records for the same entity.
A data field or attribute prioritized for governance and quality because of high business or compliance impact.
Core shared data about key business entities such as customers, products, suppliers, or locations.
Controlled lists and codes used to classify or validate other data, such as country or currency codes.
Disciplines and technologies for creating consistent, stewarded views of master entities across systems.
A reconciled, trusted representation of a master entity assembled from multiple sources using matching and survivorship rules.
Rules that decide which source value wins when conflicting attributes are merged into a master record.
Processes and patterns that move, combine, or expose data across systems so consumers receive aligned inputs.
The ability of systems and datasets to exchange and make use of information through shared formats and interfaces.
The blueprint of data structures, platforms, and flows designed to support enterprise strategy.
A structured representation of entities, attributes, and relationships at conceptual, logical, or physical levels.
Controls and practices that protect data confidentiality, integrity, and appropriate availability.
Protecting stored data by encoding it so unauthorized parties cannot read it without keys.
Protecting data while it moves across networks using secure protocols.
Granting people and systems only the minimum access required for their legitimate tasks.
A contractual or policy instrument describing allowed uses, protections, and responsibilities when data is shared between parties.
Long-term retention of selected data in durable, documented form for continuing legal, scientific, or business value.
Irreversible removal of data from relevant systems and media according to policy when retention ends.
The Data Management Capability Assessment Model from the EDM Association—used to assess and improve data management capabilities.
ISACA’s framework for governance and management of enterprise information and technology.
Maturity-oriented approaches used in some programs to score how repeatable and optimized processes are; often paired with frameworks that define what practices should exist.
An international standards family associated with data quality and related concepts; organizations may align practices to it in regulated contexts.
Practices and tools that turn curated analytical data into reports, dashboards, and insights for decision-makers.
A business-friendly mapping of metrics and entities that sits between raw data structures and analytical consumers.
A curated, documented, and governed data asset packaged for specific consumers with clear ownership and SLAs.
A score boundary that separates automatic links, steward review, and non-matches when comparing records.
A match that treats two different real-world entities as the same one, often from a weak shared clue such as a household phone.
The controlled reversal of a merge, restoring distinct identities and notifying consumers that relied on the combined record.
The stored mapping from a golden record back to the source systems and keys that contributed to it.
A governed parent-child structure among master entities, such as SKU to style to class, used for rollup and accountability.
Recording when a value or relationship starts and ends so history stays true after a change.
The designated authoritative system for a domain. Other copies are downstream, not competing sources of truth.
The operational list of exceptions—match proposals, validation failures, change requests—that stewards work to a service level.
